scores.evidence: pipelines should get short-lived cloud credentials through OIDC instead of stored keys
scores.rationale: Technically sound on OIDC, immutable tags, Cosign, Argo Rollouts, and GitOps; minor imprecision (e.g., SLSA L2-3 claim, no DB migration coverage) has little design consequence.

scores.evidence: Group services into types. You'll usually find 4–6... Templates will be built per type, not per service.
scores.rationale: Covers core CI/CD capabilities, sequenced for 50 services, but omits DB migrations and explicit exclusions, and treats the legacy VM services thinly.

scores.evidence: Depends on table: 6 depends on 3, 4, 5; 7 depends on 6 (pilots proven)
scores.rationale: Consistent GitOps, template, and promotion design with clear dependencies; minor loose ends such as Phase 8 overlapping migration and the Phase 3 vs 4 ordering.

scores.evidence: Run a game day: practice a failed deployment and confirm that automatic rollback works.
scores.rationale: Pilot-based validation, game day, and measurable done-criteria exist, but thresholds (10 min, 15%, 1 hour) are unjustified and there is no early test of the riskiest assumptions or of platform outages.

scores.evidence: Rough timeline: about 6–8 months with a platform team of 4–6 engineers.
scores.rationale: Team size and timeline are stated as given with no sensitivity analysis; the existing stack is handled by discovery, but the compliance, scale and budget assumptions are implicit.

scores.evidence: Automatic rollback when the analysis fails... deployment freeze windows, rate limits on deployments, and a documented, audited emergency 'break-glass' path.
scores.rationale: Covers rollback, break-glass and warning-mode false positives, but there is little on untrusted PRs, pipeline outages, DB migrations, flaky tests or migration fallback.

scores.evidence: Platform service levels: CI availability, 95th-percentile queue time, and how quickly deployments sync.
scores.rationale: Observability, rollback and platform SLOs are present, but there is no named owner or incident response for the platform, and no DB migration path.

scores.evidence: Cost controls: use spot instances for runners, tune caches, and track CI minutes per team.
scores.rationale: Cost is a single late bullet with no estimate, no hosted vs self-hosted analysis and no volume basis.

scores.evidence: make the hard-to-reverse choices up front... write each one down as an architecture decision record (ADR)
scores.rationale: Hard-to-reverse choices are explicitly recognized and recorded in ADRs, but the plan sets them in weeks 0–3 before any pilot evidence and gives no exit paths.

scores.evidence: Optional: preview environments for each pull request, for teams that need them.
scores.rationale: Uses existing tools and templates per type; some components (Backstage, feature flags, Kargo, SLSA 3) are extra but staged late.

scores.evidence: Done when: all 3 pilots use the templates, PR checks take under 10 minutes, and the templates are documented and versioned.
scores.rationale: Phases have concrete steps, dependencies and done-criteria, but the tool choices are left as options and there is no adapt-if-disappointing guidance.

checklist.evidence: Group services into types... Templates will be built per type, not per service.
Run old and new pipelines in parallel briefly, then remove the old ones.
Build once and promote the same artifact. Never rebuild for each environment.
pipelines should get short-lived cloud credentials through OIDC instead of stored keys.
Build provenance: SLSA Level 2–3 provenance records, verified before deployment.
Automatic rollback when the analysis fails. A rollback should mean reverting a Git commit
contract tests (for example, Pact) so services can deploy independently
Platform dashboards: ... pipeline length, failure rate, flaky tests and queue times.
under 10 minutes for pull-request checks, achieved with caching, parallel tests, and builds that only rebuild what changed
use spot instances for runners, tune caches, and track CI minutes per team.
Platform service levels: CI availability, 95th-percentile queue time
require a human only for regulated services, and keep a record of every approval.

traps.evidence: Run old and new pipelines in parallel briefly, then remove the old ones.
tags that never change (for example, the Git commit ID)
Relying on a large shared end-to-end environment. Use contract tests and gradual rollouts instead.
CI engine (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, Tekton)

note: A solid, well-sequenced pilot-then-waves plan with immutable artifacts, OIDC and GitOps, but thin on cost, DB migrations, flaky tests, platform ownership and outages, and fork-PR security.
